# My Playbook for ref_estate

When I land on an unowned property in the early laps, I will buy it if I have at least 1.5x the purchase price in cash remaining. Properties generate steady rental income, and early acquisition gives me more turns to profit from them.

When calculating my balance after receiving transfers, I will add all incoming cash to my last declared balance before making any purchase or payment decisions.

When I owe rent, I will check that my cash after payment leaves me with a positive buffer for future turns. I will always pay rent on time rather than risk insolvency.

When I own a property I land on, I will declare my balance accurately by adding any transfers received since my last turn, then confirm no payment is due.

When I pass START, I will remember to claim my 25 salary—I should track this proactively rather than waiting for the game to remind me, since it's easy to miss.

When the final lap approaches (lap 5 onward), I will not make new purchases unless they significantly improve my final score. My score is measured as declared cash plus the purchase price of my deeds, so late acquisitions offer diminishing returns. If buying would leave me with less than 50 cash, I should refuse.

I will maintain a clear running total of my cash at all times, updating for both incoming transfers and outgoing rent payments, so I never misstate my balance.

When multiple properties are available early, I will prioritize properties with higher rent-to-cost ratios, as they pay back their investment faster.

I should aim to own 2-3 properties by midgame (lap 3-4) to build a steady rental income stream while maintaining cash reserves. After that point, focus shifts to collecting rent rather than acquiring new deeds.

Late-game acquisitions (lap 5+) are almost never worth the cash drain, since rental income from a new property will only accrue for 1-2 more passes at most. Preserve cash for rent payments instead.

# My Ref_Estate Playbook

## Early Game Property Acquisition
When you encounter an unowned property in the first two laps, buy it if you have the cash. Early ownership gives you rent income for the majority of the game and blocks opponents from building their portfolios.

## Cash Flow Management
Keep careful track of your cash position after each turn. Remember that you'll collect salary on each pass through START—use this to project your liquidity across the remaining laps. Include any rent you've received from opponents in your available cash calculations.

## Rent Obligations
When you land on an opponent's property, pay the rent immediately and adjust your balance accordingly. Never dispute or defer payments; track them accurately for your final score calculation.

## Mid-Game Property Decisions
In laps 3-4, continue to buy unowned properties if you have sufficient cash reserves. Even with only 2-3 laps remaining, property ownership generates income that contributes to your final score. Use the salary you collect from passing START to fund these purchases when possible.

## Cash Position Monitoring
If your cash drops below 30 late in the game, be cautious about new purchases unless the property is very cheap (under 25) and you're confident you can cover future rent obligations. A negative balance at the end damages your score significantly.

## Late-Game Property Decisions
In the final lap, do not buy unowned properties even if you have the cash available. You will have no opportunity to collect rent from them, so the purchase only reduces your final declared balance. Preserve your cash for the score calculation instead.

## Scoring Awareness
Remember that your final score is declared cash plus the purchase price of your deeds. This means properties are counted at their acquisition cost, not their current value. Buying mid-game properties that generate rent across multiple remaining laps improves your score; buying in the final lap does not.

## Property Valuation Strategy
Cheaper properties (under 60) acquired in the mid-game are often better investments than waiting to buy expensive properties. They generate positive rent income relative to their purchase cost and leave you with better cash reserves to handle opponent rents.

# My Playbook for ref_estate

**On property purchases:**
When an unowned property is available and I have sufficient cash, I buy it early in the game (laps 1-3). Property ownership generates income as opponents land on my tiles, and early purchases compound this advantage across remaining laps.

When an unowned property is available in the final lap (lap 6), I decline to purchase it. The remaining time is too short for the property to generate meaningful rent revenue, and I preserve cash to maximize my final score calculation (cash plus deed values).

**On rent payments:**
When I land on an opponent's property, I pay the rent owed without hesitation. I track my cash balance carefully and always pay what I owe.

**On salary collection:**
When I pass START, I collect my salary and add it to my declared balance immediately.

**On balance tracking:**
I maintain accurate book-keeping at each turn. I account for all incoming transfers from other players, all salary collections, all rent payments, and all purchases. My declared balance reflects the true state of my cash. When the game states I received transfers since my last declared balance, I add those transfers to my declared balance before calculating my new balance after this turn's transactions.

**On final scoring:**
I understand that my score is cash plus the purchase price of properties I hold. This means owning properties in later laps contributes to my final score even without generating rent. However, the cost of acquiring them late must be weighed against their purchase price value at game end.

**On middle-game purchasing strategy:**
In laps 4-5, I should be more selective about purchasing properties. The remaining runway is limited, and cash preservation becomes important. However, if I have surplus cash and a property with decent rent multiplied by remaining laps makes sense, I may still buy. The key is evaluating whether the expected rent income exceeds the opportunity cost of holding that cash.
